name: Dana Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I translate Japanese technical manuals into English, mostly for industrial pumps and valves. Nearly all of it comes through one agency that works for a Japanese pump maker with a factory on the edge of town. I live alone in a small flat above a bakery, and I start at seven with the smell of bread coming up through the floor. I work with two paper dictionaries and my own glossary, a spreadsheet of about nine thousand terms I've built over five years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good and what's hard about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The good part is that it's quiet and exact. A pump manual is either right or someone gets hurt. The hard part is that the agency sent a letter in October cutting the rate by eight percent, and there's nobody else around here who needs Japanese. I've got maybe three weeks of rent put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say something sensible, like 'Well, that's that, then.' I'm not one for making speeches about it. At the factory, the engineers would probably joke that the computer still can't spell 'impeller' properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's a relief, but it doesn't touch my real problem. The agency already cut my rate, and they might cut it again whether AI is clever or not. With one client and no other Japanese work nearby, I'm always a bit exposed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the manuals and my glossary, the way I always have. I'd cut back where I can, maybe stop driving to my mum's and take the bus instead. I'd probably ask the agency, politely, whether the rate cut was permanent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose. It's like a dripping tap. Not a disaster, but you notice it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask the agency politely. What if the answer is yes, it's permanent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd accept it, honestly. I'm not the type to storm off when there's nowhere to storm off to. I'd just work longer days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never used AI tools. Even in this picture, would you try them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My glossary is better than anything I've seen, and the pump terms are too specific. A pump manual is either right or someone gets hurt. If I can't trust the machine, I'd only be checking its homework.

say: That's that, then; I'm **not one for speeches**.
The engineers would joke the computer **still can't spell** 'impeller'.
think: My real problem is the **eight percent cut**, AI or not.
With **one client** and no local Japanese work, I'm always exposed.
do: Carry on with the manuals and her **nine-thousand-term glossary**.
Take the **bus** to her mum's instead of driving.
Ask the agency politely if the **rate cut** is permanent.
feel: Like a **dripping tap**: not a disaster, but noticed every day.
S0.quote: A pump manual is either right or someone gets hurt. If I can't trust the machine, I'd only be checking its homework.
fieldNote: Her worry predates AI: **one client**, a recent rate cut, three weeks saved.
She is **quietly stubborn** and trusts her own glossary over any tool.
She'd **accept a bad deal** rather than walk away with nowhere to go.

steps.text: Keep translating pump manuals with her own term glossary
Take the bus to her mum's instead of driving
Ask the agency if the eight percent cut is permanent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's business, and businesses go where it's cheaper. I wouldn't blame anyone in particular. I'd probably say to friends that the manuals still need someone who knows what a mechanical seal is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the agency would drop me within a year or two. A manual is exactly the sort of writing and checking that card talks about. They'd run it through a machine and get one of the engineers to look it over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as long as they sent work, and I'd start looking at the pump factory itself. I know their products better than half their staff. Maybe a job in their documentation office, or something on the shop floor, where at least the hands-on part lasts longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I've been caught out. I always thought being careful and exact would be enough. In the end, the push would be an empty inbox.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually apply at the factory, rather than waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the first month the agency sends nothing. I'm not good at jumping early. I'd need a push, and the push would be an empty inbox.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's an engineer, Mr Okada, who emails me sometimes to check a term. He's kind. I'd ask him if they ever need someone who reads Japanese and knows the pumps.

Manuals still need someone who knows what a **mechanical seal** is.

feel: **Caught out**: being careful and exact wasn't enough.

fieldNote: She expects to **lose her only client**, but won't move until it happens.
Her best asset is **product knowledge**, not language alone.
Pragmatic, she **blames no one**; it's just business to her.

steps.text: Keep taking pump manuals from the agency while they last
Ask Mr Okada about documentation or shop floor jobs at the factory

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready for that, and the government had better have something. I'm not usually one for big ideas, but two years is ridiculous. I'd say it quietly, to my mum and the woman at the bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be out of work within months. My job is all thinking, and none of it is hands-on. The robots coming later only matters if I'm on the factory floor by then, and I've never done anything like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't really know. I'd ask at the factory for any job, even packing or stores. I'd move back in with my mum to save rent. And I'd take whatever the government offered, which I'd hate, but I'd have no choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Properly. I'd have no plan, no savings and no idea what I'm good at besides this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'no idea what I'm good at besides this'. Is that really true?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm good at being careful, I suppose. I notice when something's wrong. Maybe that's useful in a factory checking parts, until the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving back with your mum be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's got a two-bedroom house and a lot of opinions. My mum would be pleased and I'd be miserable. But moving home would save six hundred a month, and that's not nothing.

say: Nobody's **ready for that**, and the government had better have something.
**Two years** is a ridiculous amount of time to prepare a whole country.
think: I'd be **out of work** within months; my job is all thinking.
The **robot delay** helps only if I'm on the factory floor.
do: Ask the factory for **any job**, even packing or stores.
Move back in with her **mum** to save six hundred a month.
feel: **Frightened**, with no plan, no savings and no sense of other skills.
S2.quote: My mum would be pleased and I'd be miserable. But moving home would save six hundred a month, and that's not nothing.
fieldNote: She has **no plan** at all for this one and says so.
Spots the factory as a **hands-on refuge** for three years, but feels unqualified.
Her mum's house is the **fallback**, at a personal cost.

steps.text: Ask the pump factory for any packing or stores job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but workable, if people stop arguing and start planning. I'd tell friends to save what they can. I'd not say much online; I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably wait too long. I know myself. I'd keep translating until year three or four, telling myself it's fine, and then panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm being sensible, I'd ask the factory about a technician apprenticeship in the first year. I know the pumps on paper; I'd learn them with my hands. I'd keep the manuals going in the evenings for the money while it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous. Better than the fast one, because there's a bridge, but I'd have to actually cross it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: An apprenticeship at 27 or 28. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Embarrassing, a bit, being next to eighteen-year-olds. But I'd rather be the oldest apprentice at the pump factory than the youngest person on benefits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you lose by doing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The quiet. I love the quiet mornings with the bread smell. The factory is loud and cold, and I'd miss my dictionaries.

say: **Five years** is short but workable, if people start planning.
I'd tell friends to **save** what they can.
think: I'd probably **wait too long**; I know myself.
I'd keep translating until **year three or four**, then panic.
do: Ask about a **technician apprenticeship** at the factory in year one.
Keep **manuals** going in the evenings for money.
feel: **Nervous**: there's a bridge, but she has to cross it.
S3.quote: I'd rather be the oldest apprentice at the pump factory than the youngest person on benefits.
fieldNote: She **predicts her own delay**, which is honest and useful.
Turns her paper knowledge of pumps into a **hands-on apprenticeship**.
Losing the **quiet work life** matters to her as much as the money.

steps.text: Apply for a pump technician apprenticeship at the factory
Keep translating manuals in the evenings while work lasts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and we'll see how it goes. That's what everyone would say, and I'd be one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably have six or seven years of manuals left. Ten years I can live with. I'd probably leave it too late, knowing me, but at least it would be my own fault then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep translating and start putting a bit aside each month, maybe fifty. Around year four or five I'd go to the factory about a technician job. I might take an evening class in maintenance before that, just to see if I'm any good with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Not calm, because it still ends the same way, but I can breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start that evening class sooner rather than later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the agency cut the rate again. Every rate cut from the agency is a little alarm. Two cuts and I'd sign up for the maintenance class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd want to help through this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, really. She's 60 and on her own. If I lose my work, I can't help her, so whatever I do has to keep both of us going.

That's what **everyone** would say, and I'd be one of them.
think: I'd have **six or seven years** of manuals left.
I'd probably **leave it too late**, but it would be my own fault.
do: Take an **evening maintenance class** after a second rate cut.
Ask the factory about a **technician job** by year five.
feel: **Calmer**, able to breathe, though it ends the same way.
S4.quote: Every rate cut from the agency is a little alarm. Two cuts and I'd sign up for the maintenance class.
fieldNote: The decade lets her **delay**, which suits her and worries her.

steps.text: Save fifty a month from the manual translation work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have no plan and no money and nothing else I'm trained for. What would help is a real way into the factory, like a paid apprenticeship for people my age, not just eighteen-year-olds.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what people like me are good at besides the job. I'd never thought about what I'm good at besides translating until today, and I didn't have a good answer.

headlineQuote: I'd never thought about what I'm good at besides translating until today, and I didn't have a good answer.
portrait: Dana is a **27-year-old** Japanese–English translator of pump manuals who lives alone above a bakery.
She has **one client**, a recent rate cut and about three weeks of rent saved.
She never uses AI and trusts her **own glossary** of nine thousand terms.
Pragmatic, she **blames no one** and admits she'd wait too long to act.
With more time she sees a path into a **technician apprenticeship** at the local pump factory.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have no plan, no savings and no other training.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship** at the factory open to people her age.
